sections.Overview: Good stories start with something you have never done. Get to know your friends, one confession at a time. This guide uses a clearly defined four-player house version; regional rules may differ.
sections.Setup:
1. Sit in a circle and agree on subjects everyone is comfortable discussing.
2. Choose a starting player; play moves clockwise. Decide on three full laps.
sections.How to Play:
1. The starter makes a true statement beginning “Never have I ever…” For example: “Never have I ever missed a flight.”
2. Everyone who HAS done that thing raises a hand. Sharing the story is optional. The speaker does not respond to their own true statement.
3. The next player invents a new statement. Anyone may pass or replace an uncomfortable prompt without explanation.
sections.Drinking Rules: Players who have done the thing may take one optional small sip per statement, or simply raise a hand. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: Finish after three full laps, or whenever the group wants. There is no required winner.
sections.Optional Variations: Ten Fingers: everyone starts with ten fingers up and lowers one for each applicable statement. First to zero ends the game; remaining fingers are the score. Try a five-finger mini game or themed prompts.
sections.Four-Player Notes: With four, allow time for stories between statements. Avoid using prompts to single out one person.

sections.Setup:
1. Sit where everyone can point at everyone else.
2. Take turns inventing lighthearted “Who is most likely to…?” questions; agree on ten prompts.
sections.How to Play:
1. The starting reader asks a question, such as “Who is most likely to adopt five dogs?”
2. Count down from three and point simultaneously. Everyone chooses one person; self-voting is allowed in this house version.
3. Count votes. The most-voted player gets one point. Tied players each get a point, with no repeat vote.
4. Rotate the reader clockwise and ask a new question.
sections.Drinking Rules: At most one optional sip for a most-voted player, regardless of votes. Ties need no drinking penalty. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: After ten questions, the person with most points wins the unofficial superlative crown. Ties share the title.
sections.Optional Variations: Use themes such as travel, cooking, or fictional survival. Play the minority-vote version or swap sips for harmless challenges.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Four votes often tie; agree to share the result rather than escalating penalties.

sections.Setup:
1. Choose a starter and a category with many answers, such as countries, pasta shapes, or movie titles.
2. Agree on a five-second answer window and play five rounds.
sections.How to Play:
1. The starter names the category and gives the first valid example.
2. Proceed clockwise. Each player gives a new example within five seconds; repeats within that round are not allowed.
3. An invalid answer, repeated answer, or timeout ends the round. Settle disputed answers by group agreement; replay a disputed turn without penalty.
4. The player who ended the round chooses the next category and starts it. Record one loss for that player.
sections.Drinking Rules: The player who loses a category may take one small sip at the round boundary, or take a point instead. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: Finish after five categories. Fewest lost rounds wins; ties share the win.
sections.Optional Variations: Use a three-second timer, alphabetical answers, or a steady spoken beat. For example: France → Japan → Brazil → France ends the round.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Rotate between broad and niche categories so one expert does not control every round.

sections.Setup:
1. Choose a starter and begin clockwise with the phrase “fuzzy duck.”
2. Agree on a three-second response window and eight rounds.
sections.How to Play:
1. The active player says “fuzzy duck” to pass play to the next person in the current direction.
2. Instead, they may say “does he?” This reverses direction and changes the active phrase to “ducky fuzz.” The previous player now acts.
3. Another “does he?” reverses direction again and changes the phrase back to “fuzzy duck.”
4. A wrong phrase, muddled pronunciation, or timeout ends the round. The player who made the error restarts clockwise with “fuzzy duck.”
sections.Drinking Rules: One optional small sip at the end of a lost round. No doubling for accidentally saying something funny. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: After eight rounds, fewest errors wins. Count errors with fingers or paper if desired.
sections.Optional Variations: Use a two-second response window or invent another reversal phrase. Decide whether immediate consecutive reversals are allowed; this version allows them.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Track both the phrase and direction; the person who just spoke may immediately receive the turn back.

2. Keep the gaze fixed until the result is clear. Any two people looking at one another form a mutual pair.
3. Each member of a mutual pair receives one point. Two pairs can match in the same round. If no gazes match, no points are awarded.
4. Look down again and rotate the caller clockwise.

sections.Overview: One deck, a table full of mini-games, and a new twist on every turn. The game-night classic, reimagined. This guide uses a clearly defined four-player house version; regional rules may differ.
sections.What You Need:
- Standard 52-card deck
- Empty cup or marker
sections.Setup:
1. Shuffle a standard deck and spread it face down around an empty central cup or marker. No shared drink is needed.
2. Choose a starter. Read the house rule map below aloud before drawing.
sections.How to Play:
1. Draw one card clockwise, announce its rank, and perform that rank’s action. Discard the card afterward.
2. Use this explicit low-intensity HOUSE MAP: **A:** last hand raised gets a point. **2:** ask another player a trivia question; incorrect gets a point. **3:** drawer gets a point. **4:** last to touch the floor gets a point.
3. **5:** drawer becomes thumb master until the next five; once, place a thumb on the table and last to copy gets a point. **6:** create one harmless table rule, expiring at the next six. **7:** last to raise a hand gets a point.
4. **8:** pick a teammate for the next mini-game, without duplicated penalties. **9:** start a clockwise rhyming chain; first repeat or five-second pause gets a point. **10:** play [Categories](#game/categories).
5. **J:** make one Never Have I Ever statement; applicable players get a point. **Q:** start a questions-only chain; an answer, repeat, or five-second pause gets a point. **K:** add one harmless rule; the fourth King ends the game.
6. A mini-game produces at most one point per player. A forgotten ongoing rule never stacks with another consequence from that card.
sections.Drinking Rules: Optional house overlay: replace a point with at most one small sip, or keep all points. Traditional waterfalls, gender rules, shared drinks, and escalating quantities are replaced here. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: Stop at the fourth King or when the deck runs out. Fewest points wins. No one finishes the central cup.
sections.Optional Variations: Kings and Ring of Fire are aliases. Use half a deck for a shorter session; swap any uncomfortable action for a compliment or charades.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Four players get many turns. Keep the rule map open and allow free passes for physical actions.

sections.Overview: Read the cards, clear the pyramid, and see who catches the last bus home. This guide uses a clearly defined four-player house version; regional rules may differ.
sections.Setup:
1. Choose a dealer. Shuffle 52 cards; keep Aces high, and agree that equal ranks lose prediction guesses.
2. House version: deal each player four cards through the guessing sequence, then build a 15-card pyramid in rows of 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 from the remaining deck.
sections.How to Play:
1. Starting left of the dealer, each player predicts red or black before their first card is revealed. Keep each revealed card in front of its owner.
2. For card two, guess higher or lower than card one. For card three, guess strictly inside or outside the ranks of the first two; equality loses. If the first two tie, only outside can win. For card four, guess a suit. Correct guesses earn a point.
3. Reveal the pyramid bottom row first, one card at a time. Any player holding the same rank may discard one matching card. There are no row multipliers or bluffing in this house version.
4. The player with most cards remaining rides the bus. Break ties with lowest prediction score, then a random draw.
5. Limited bus HOUSE RULE: that player makes four new red/black predictions from the remaining deck, recording successes. No resets; the bus ends after four cards.
sections.Drinking Rules: Score prediction misses with tokens. Optional alcohol overlay: only the final rider may take one small sip after the bus. No repeated or escalating drinking. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: The bus ends after exactly four guesses. Fewest cards remaining wins the pyramid; the rider tries to earn at least two correct bus guesses.
sections.Optional Variations: Skip the final bus or play pyramid only. Regional bus and pyramid layouts vary; the fixed-attempt version here deliberately replaces restart-based endings.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Rotate the dealer for another session so everyone participates in setup.

sections.Overview: Ten cards stand between you and the finish. The catch? This bridge has a habit of growing. This guide uses a clearly defined four-player house version; regional rules may differ.
sections.Setup:
1. Shuffle 52 cards and place ten face-down cards in a line. Keep the rest as a draw pile.
2. Dealer’s left starts. Set a 15-minute house time limit.
sections.How to Play:
1. Flip from the near end of the bridge. A number card from 2–10 is safe: discard it and continue flipping.
2. A Jack, Queen, King, or Ace ends the turn. Discard it and add respectively 1, 2, 3, or 4 face-down cards to the far end.
3. Pass clockwise. The next player continues at the remaining bridge; do not restart already cleared cards.
4. If the draw pile runs out, shuffle discards. The person clearing the final card wins.
sections.Drinking Rules: Any face card or Ace may cost one optional sip, independent of how many cards it adds. Use a single round-end token penalty instead for slower pacing. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: End when the bridge is cleared. At the 15-minute house limit, stop cooperatively and record how many cards remain.
sections.Optional Variations: Individual attempts or a cooperative bridge are alternatives. For a points variant, award one point for each safe card cleared.

1. Before revealing the next card, say “higher” or “lower” relative to the face-up card.
2. Turn the card over. A correct prediction earns one point; a miss or equal rank earns zero.
3. The newly revealed card becomes the reference card, regardless of the result. Pass to the next person immediately.
4. When the deck runs out, reshuffle discards while keeping the reference card visible.
sections.Drinking Rules: A wrong call may cost one optional small sip. Never make the same player keep guessing until correct; points-only is equally playable. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: After everyone has made eight predictions, highest score wins. Ties share the win.

sections.Overview: A little aim, a little teamwork, and a whole lot of “that absolutely went in.”
sections.What You Need:
- 20 cups with water
- 2 ping-pong balls
- Table
sections.Setup:
1. Make two teams of two. Set ten cups in a tight triangle at each end of a stable table; partially fill them with water for weight. Keep personal drinks separate.
2. Use two clean ping-pong balls. House rules below simplify tournament rules; agree on who shoots first.
sections.How to Play:
1. Starting team takes one shot, then each subsequent turn gives each teammate one throw toward the opposing cups.
2. A ball landing and staying in a cup removes that cup after the turn. If both balls land in the same cup, count one cup only in this simplified version.
3. Once per game, each team may ask for its opponents’ remaining cups to be rearranged tightly at the start of its turn. No bounce bonuses or swatting in this version.
4. After a team clears the final cup, the opponents get one redemption turn with one shot each. Clearing all remaining cups ties the game.
5. On a tie, reset three cups per side and play another round using the same rules.
sections.Drinking Rules: Custom overlay: after an opposing scoring turn, the defending team may share at most one optional small sip total. Never drink target-cup water. Points-only play is identical. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: The team clearing the opponents’ cups wins after redemption fails. If repeated ties occur, agree on a final one-cup sudden-death round with equal turns.
sections.Optional Variations: Use six cups for shorter play. Published rules differ on bounce shots, same-cup shots, re-racks, and redemption; agree before starting. Tournament water-cup rules are linked for reference.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Two throws per ordinary team turn gives each teammate equal participation. Separate drinks keep gameplay independent of consumption.

sections.Overview: Two teams, eight bags, and just enough friendly trash talk. Take game night outside.
sections.Setup:
1. Place two cornhole boards facing each other on level ground. Official distance is 27 feet between front edges; agree on a shorter casual distance if needed.
2. Each team has four bags of a distinct color. One teammate stands at each board, next to an opponent. Choose first throw by coin toss.
sections.How to Play:
1. The two players at one end alternate throwing all eight bags toward the other board, staying behind the front edge.
2. A bag through the hole scores three; a bag on the board scores one; off-board scores zero. Score after all eight bags land.
3. Use cancellation scoring: subtract the lower team total from the higher. Only the difference is added to the winning team’s running score. Example: 7 versus 4 gives three points.
4. The partners at the other board play the next frame. The team scoring in the previous frame throws first; if tied, retain the order.
sections.Drinking Rules: Custom overlay: each losing teammate may choose one small sip after the completed game. No penalties per throw or point. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: First team to reach or exceed 21 at the end of a completed frame wins; no exact-21 bust rule.
sections.Optional Variations: Play best of three, shorten throwing distance, or give a beginner team a starting-point handicap.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Official doubles is exactly 2v2. Teammates stay at opposite ends so all four take part every two frames.

sections.Overview: One word can connect everything. A clever 2v2 battle of clues, connections, and dangerous guesses.
sections.Setup:
1. Use the Codenames set. Lay out 25 random word cards in a 5×5 grid. Split into two teams, each with a spymaster and guesser.
2. Only spymasters see the key showing team words, bystanders, and assassin. The key indicates which team starts and has the extra agent.
sections.How to Play:
1. The active spymaster gives one word and a number, connecting that many of their team’s words. A clue must concern meanings, not visible spelling or position.
2. Their teammate touches one word at a time. Spymasters cover each chosen card according to the key, keeping faces neutral.
3. A correct team agent permits another guess. The guesser may stop, and can make at most the clue number plus one guesses.
4. A bystander or opponent’s agent ends the turn; an assassin guess immediately loses the game. Continue alternating clues.
sections.Drinking Rules: Custom overlay: each losing teammate may choose one small sip at game end. Wrong guesses do not automatically cost drinks. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: Reveal all your team’s agents before the other team, or win immediately when the other team selects the assassin.
sections.Optional Variations: Swap spymasters after every game. Codenames Pictures uses picture cards and a 4×5 grid with its own key/set; use the same clue-and-guess loop and consult that edition’s rules.

sections.Overview: Match colors, reverse the mood, and remember that one very important word.
sections.Setup:
1. Use a classic UNO deck. Deal seven cards to each player; place the rest face down and flip a starting discard, following the deck’s rules for opening action cards.
2. House opening: reveal cards until a number card appears as the starting discard, return skipped actions to the draw pile, and reshuffle it. Dealer’s left starts clockwise. Draw penalties cannot be stacked.
sections.How to Play:
1. Play one card matching the top discard’s color, number, or symbol; a Wild lets you choose the next color.
2. If you cannot or choose not to play, draw one card. You may play that card if legal; otherwise your turn ends.
3. Skip misses the next player; Reverse changes direction. Draw Two makes the next player draw two and miss their turn. Draw penalties are not stacked.
4. Wild Draw Four is legal only when you have no card matching the current color; the next player draws four and misses their turn. A challenge checks that legality: an illegal user draws four instead; a failed challenger draws six.
5. Say “UNO” as you play your second-to-last card. If caught before the next player begins, draw two. First to empty their hand wins the round.
sections.Drinking Rules: Custom overlay: a player who draws because they cannot play may choose one small sip for that entire turn, independent of cards drawn. Alternative: only the highest remaining hand after a round may sip. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: For a quick session, play three rounds and count wins. Official long-form scoring awards opponents’ remaining cards to the winner (numbers face value, actions 20, Wilds 50), racing to 500.
sections.Optional Variations: Play two partnerships with partners opposite. Blank Wild house rules depend on the owned edition; agree before dealing.
sections.Four-Player Notes: Four is within classic UNO’s 2–10 range. Action cards affect only the next player unless the deck explicitly says otherwise.

1. Build the 54-block tower: three blocks per level, alternating directions between levels.
2. Optional house variant: number selected blocks and prepare a separate prompt sheet, mostly non-drinking tasks. The builder starts.
sections.How to Play:
1. Using only one hand at a time, remove one block from below the highest completed level. You may gently test blocks; return displaced ones before trying another.
2. Place the removed block on top, perpendicular to the previous level, completing a three-block level before starting another.
3. If using the prompt sheet, read and optionally complete the removed block’s instruction. Harmless examples: compliment someone, reverse turn order, or name three countries.
4. Pass clockwise when the tower is stable. A turn finishes after the next player touches it, or ten seconds after placement, following classic instructions.

sections.Overview: Your living room, your quiz. Bring the odd facts and crown the group’s resident know-it-all.
sections.What You Need:
- Paper and pen per person

sections.Setup:
1. Custom format inspired by the report: prepare 12 questions in three rounds of four. Write each answer separately so players cannot see it.
2. Each player needs paper and a pen. For fair four-person play, each player prepares three questions and sits out scoring only on their own questions.
sections.How to Play:
1. Rotate the reader clockwise. The reader asks one of their prepared questions; the other three write an answer privately within 30 seconds.
2. Reveal answers together. The reader checks the prepared answer and awards one point for each correct response. Clarify acceptable wording before scoring.
3. After four questions, total that round’s scores. Every player has answered three questions and read one.
4. Repeat for three rounds. Nobody changes a question after hearing an answer. Void a factually disputed question unless the group can verify it.
sections.Drinking Rules: Optional custom overlay: only the last-place player after a full four-question round may take one small sip. Tied last places can use points instead. Always allow points, a nonalcoholic drink, or a free pass.
sections.How the Game Ends: Highest total from nine answered questions wins. Ties share victory or use a prepared closest-estimate tiebreaker.
sections.Optional Variations: Use music intros you supply, friend trivia, themed pub quiz rounds, or stretch to an hour-long quiz with round-level scoring. A shared device is optional for audio or displaying questions.
sections.Four-Player Notes: The rotating reader system keeps all four involved and gives everyone the same number of answer opportunities.

sections.How to Play:
1. Share the prediction lists before pressing play. No additions after the movie starts.
2. When a predicted event happens, its owner quietly marks it once. Repeated occurrences do not earn more points.
3. Compare lists at a natural intermission without interrupting scenes. Settle ambiguous calls by a friendly group vote.
4. At the credits, count one point for each confirmed prediction.
